newsitem.title: Russia: Six foreign aid workers gunned down in Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: Six foreign aid workers gunned down in Chechnya.

text.p: Six foreign aid workers, five of them women, were gunned down in their beds on Tuesday in the most violent incident of its kind in Russia's breakaway region of Chechnya.

Local residents watched in grim silence as colleagues loaded coffins onto a truck bearing the red and white logo of the International Committee of the Red Cross, whose workers were killed in the early morning attack in a hospital compound.

A Red Cross official in Geneva described the attack as an assassination, while some Chechen leaders said it was "political provocation" aimed at disrupting local presidential and parliamentary elections planned for January 27.
The Russian foreign ministry said it hoped the peace process would not be disrupted in the region, which Moscow is determined to keep as part of the Russian Federation.

"We are shocked, we are outraged, it is a terrible crime," spokesman Gennady Tarasov told a news conference in Moscow. "But of course we hope strongly that this criminal act will not negatively affect the peace process."

The hospital where the attack took place was opened in the village of Novye Atagi in August by the Red Cross's Norwegian branch, which said at the time it had guarantees of security from both Russian and Chechen officials.
But Red Cross officials said someone broke into the compound during the night and shot the workers as they slept.

"We are strongly condemning this attack, which is a serious violation of international humanitarian law. The hospital was clearly marked with Red Cross signs all over it," said Geneva-based spokesman Tony Burgener.
"It was an attack on their residence when they were sleeping at four a.m. this morning. It was an assassination."
Burgener said the murdered workers came from Norway, the Netherlands, Canada, Spain and New Zealand and the Red Cross was now pulling all its workers out of Chechnya.
Local people, suspicious of Russia's motives in the Caucasus region, denounced the killings.

"We are trying to investigate it, but I am convinced it is a big provocation against Chechnya, against peace in Chechnya," said a local Chechen police officer. "We are sure that Russian intelligence is involved."
"No sane person could have done this," added Ali Zabarayev, 45. "We knew these people and they worked in our village, nobody from us could have done this."

Moscow Red Cross official Thierry Meyrat said the organisation might have underestimated the impact of groups in the region which were "obviously out of control", but gave no clue to who might have shot the workers.

Tens of thousands of people have been killed in Chechnya since Russia sent troops there in December 1994 to crush an independence bid and the fighting has been punctuated by claims and counter claims about who is responsible for what.
Russian forces now have little control over what happens in Chechnya, and power is in the hands of a separatist-led "coalition" government headed by former rebel military commander Aslan Maskhadov.
Moscow's soldiers pulled out ignominiously this year after failing to crush resistence from determined guerrillas. A peace deal deferred any decision on Chechnya's status for five years.

Most of Chechnya's towns were wrecked in the fighting and aid agencies have been trying to help those left homeless or without medical services in a region where power, water and telephone communications are rare.

They have suffered a spate of kidnappings and ransom demands, most of them lasting for only a few days, and at least two aid workers have been killed -- one American and one Finnish. But this is the first incident on this scale.

Both Moscow and Chechnya's separatist leaders are trying to keep the peace settlement on track and rebel leaders have denounced hostage seizures, such as the one last Saturday when rebel commando Salman Raduyev took 21 Russian soldiers captive.
